relevance_note: Case report of a Thai man with PAMI syndrome and a PSTPIP1 variant: "identified a PSTPIP1 mutation, specifically the heterozygous E250K variant"; the Discussion also summarizes earlier PSTPIP1 cases with individual-level features.
method_note: Built by hand-written Python (build.py in scratch) from my reading; every span checked verbatim by script. In scope: the case-report patient ('patient'); his father, described with severe adolescent acne but untested (included as an affected relative; 'otherwise healthy' was not used to exclude any checklist item); and previously published people from the Discussion with individual-level facts: the p.E101G PAB case [11, 12] and the asymptomatic father carrying it, the German mother and son [14], the p.T255M case [15], the p.G403R PAC case [16], the Japanese case [17] and two Russian patients [18]. For [11, 12], [15] and [16], PG/acne/HS/fever were recorded as observed from the syndrome name the paper gives for that single case. The [14] family, [17] and [18] patients have no printed variant, so no variant rows. The [14] and [18] people have no per-person diagnosis label in the text; they are in scope from context (colitis cases in PAPA/PAMI). PSTPIP1 gene symbol for [15] and [16] is quoted from the reference titles; for p.E101G from the PAID context. p.E101G inheritance recorded as inherited paternal because the variant was identified in the patient's asymptomatic father. Patient: Table 1 is a longitudinal table with time points as columns (column header 'Baseline' used for ESR 97, CRP 92, ANC 930). Platelets (148,000 at 18 months) not called low by the paper, so thrombocytopenia not reported; 'bicytopenia' does not say which lineages. Serum calprotectin was not measured, so hypercalprotectinemia is not reported. Short stature below the 3rd percentile recorded as growth failure (observed). Age at onset left not reported: childhood abscesses at vaccination sites precede the perianal abscess at 15, and colitis began at about 21. Variant type 'missense' comes from the Introduction sentence naming E250K; functional evidence (enhanced pyrin binding) is cited from ref [1], not measured here. Negative infection tests (TB PCR, AFB, CMV, rapid urease) not recorded as features. No internal contradictions found.

Prednisolone at 1 mg/kg/day effectively increased hemoglobin levels, but the patient’s white blood cell counts remained low. To address leukopenia, the prednisolone dose was tapered to 0.5 mg/kg/day and cyclosporin 100 mg/day was added.
